The canal behind the sugar mill was running high and brown after three days of rain. Darshan stood on the railing of the little bridge, arms out, and looked down at the others.
"Aditi, you first. You always say you swim better than me."
Aditi shook her head. "Water's too fast today."
"Scared?" Darshan laughed loudly, and two younger boys laughed with him. It felt good, every face turned up toward him. "Come on, if I jump alone it's no fun."
His hand was gripping the railing so hard that his knuckles had gone pale.
Aditi picked up her cycle. "I'm going home. You should come too."
When she rode off, the younger boys drifted after her one by one. Darshan stayed on the railing a minute longer, then climbed down slowly, and nobody was there to see how relieved he looked.

qa.q: Where was the canal that Darshan wanted to jump into?
qa.a: The canal was behind the sugar mill, running high and brown after three days of rain.

qa.q: What do Darshan's pale knuckles suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: They suggest Darshan was frightened himself; daring Aditi to go first and enjoying the laughter covered his own fear and gave him a feeling of power.

qa.q: Which choice turned the moment around, and what could Darshan try next time?
qa.a: Aditi's calm refusal and leaving gave everyone a way out; next time Darshan could admit he is unsure instead of daring others to share his risk.

qa.q: How might the younger boys have seen the dare?
qa.a: At first they laughed along with Darshan, but once Aditi left they followed her, which shows they only needed someone to make leaving feel normal.

grounding: A teenage boy dares others into a risky jump because he wants company in his own fear and enjoys feeling powerful, not because they are cowards.

The rain started ten minutes before the tuition bus was due. Tanvir stood under the bus-stop roof, phone battery at nine percent, and made his decision again: no maths test today, the arcade instead. Then he turned to Lalit.
"Come on. Nobody checks attendance when it rains. Just this once."
Lalit shook his head. "I actually studied."
"You always study. Live a little, yaar."
Tanvir heard his own voice getting louder and didn't know why. The truth sat under it: if he went alone, it was just him bunking, and that felt stupid and scary. If Lalit came, it became an adventure they shared.
The bus splashed up. Lalit climbed on without another word. Tanvir stood there with wet shoes and a dying phone, suddenly very alone. After a long minute he ran through the puddles and jumped on too.

qa.q: What did Tanvir decide at the bus stop?
qa.a: Tanvir decided: no maths test today, the arcade instead.

qa.q: What was Tanvir afraid of while he kept pushing Lalit to come?
qa.a: Tanvir was scared of bunking alone; going alone felt stupid and scary, while Lalit coming would turn it into a shared adventure.

qa.q: What could Lalit keep doing if a friend pushes like this again?
qa.a: Lalit can give the same short, calm no and get on the bus; staying steady also left Tanvir a way to change his mind.

qa.q: How might the afternoon have gone if Lalit had given in?
qa.a: Both would have missed the test, and Tanvir might never have noticed that the push came from his own fear rather than from anything about Lalit.

grounding: Shows a teenager pressing a friend to bunk because going alone feels lonely and frightening, so the push reflects the pusher's own uncertainty.

On the colony's back steps after tuition, Yamini laid out the plan: the eleven o'clock show on Saturday, out through the service gate after her parents slept.
"You're coming, Madhav. Don't be a baby."
Madhav picked at his shoelace. "My mother checks my room."
"So? Everyone else is in."
Nobody else was in yet, and Yamini knew it. But when Madhav's shoulders dropped a little, she felt a small rush, the same one she got when the group waited for her to choose the snack or the song. At home this month everything was about her brother's board exams; nobody asked what she thought about anything.
Madhav stood up. "Not this one, Yamini. I'll come for the afternoon show if you want."
Her face went hot. For a second she wanted to call him boring in front of everyone. She didn't. She just said, "Whatever," and scrolled her phone, oddly shaky.

qa.q: When did Yamini plan to go to the show?
qa.a: The eleven o'clock show on Saturday, out through the service gate after her parents slept.

qa.q: What did Yamini feel when Madhav's shoulders dropped, and why might that matter to her?
qa.a: Yamini felt a small rush of power; at home everything was about her brother's board exams and nobody asked what she thought.

qa.q: Which choice worked in Madhav's answer?
qa.a: Madhav gave a short, calm no and offered the afternoon show instead, so he stayed friendly without joining the risky plan.

qa.q: How might the others on the steps see Yamini's push if they knew nobody else was in yet?
qa.a: They might see that 'everyone else is in' was not true, and that the pressure was about Yamini's need to feel in charge, not about Madhav.

grounding: Shows a teenager pushing a friend toward a risky night out because making others follow gives her a feeling of power she lacks at home.

On the coaching centre's back staircase, Rehana blocked the way down.
"Just quit with me. Tell your dad the coaching is useless."
"It isn't useless for me," Harish said. "I like the physics sir."
"You'll fail the entrance anyway. Everyone does."
"Why do you care so much if I stay?"
"I don't care."
"You've asked me four times since Monday."
Rehana looked at the wall. "Because if it's just me, then it's just me who messed up. If you quit too, it's a decision. Two people can't both be wrong."
"They can, actually."
"Wow. Thanks."
"I'm not leaving," Harish said. "But I'll sit with you when you tell your parents, if you want."
She was quiet for a moment. "I haven't told them anything."
"I know. That's the scary part, na?"
Rehana let out a breath and finally moved aside.

qa.q: How many times had Rehana asked Harish since Monday?
qa.a: Rehana had asked Harish four times since Monday.

qa.q: What was Rehana worried about underneath the pushing?
qa.a: Rehana was scared of being the only one who messed up; if Harish quit too, it would feel like a decision instead of a lonely mistake.

qa.q: What small step did Harish offer instead of joining?
qa.a: Harish offered to sit with Rehana when she tells her parents, keeping his own no firm while nudging her toward honesty with trusted adults.

qa.q: How might Rehana's parents feel if they learned about the quitting from someone else first?
qa.a: They would likely feel hurt by the secret more than by the choice itself, which is why telling them herself, with support, matters.

grounding: Shows a teenager pressing a friend to quit with her because doing it alone makes her own choice feel frightening and wrong.

passage: Looking back at last term, I think I was the one doing the pushing, not the one being pushed. I'd decided to skip maths tuition every Thursday to hang out at the arcade. I hadn't told Abba, and every Thursday my stomach churned on the walk there. So I started on Harsha. "Come on, one day. Don't be a baby. Everyone skips." I said it again and again, louder each week. When Harsha finally said, "Fine, just this once," I felt a rush, like I'd won something. That should have told me something. Honestly, it wasn't about Harsha at all. If Harsha came, I wasn't the only one breaking the rule, or the only one who'd get caught. And for a second I felt big instead of scared. The next Thursday Harsha said no, quietly, and walked into tuition. I stood outside for a minute, then followed. I, Farhan, still haven't said why I pushed so hard. Maybe I'll start with this.

qa.q: Where did Farhan go instead of maths tuition?
qa.a: To hang out at the arcade.

qa.q: Why did Farhan push Harsha so hard?
qa.a: Farhan felt scared and alone in the risky choice; getting Harsha to join meant not being the only one, and for a second Farhan felt big instead of scared.

qa.q: What could Farhan do now?
qa.a: Farhan could tell Harsha honestly why the pushing happened and apologise, and talk to Abba about the skipped Thursdays.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt being called a baby each week?
qa.a: Harsha likely felt pressured and small, which is why the “fine, just this once” came, before a quiet no the next week.

grounding: Shows a teenager pressing a friend to join a risky choice to feel less alone and more powerful, driven by the pusher's own uncertainty.
